Testimony of Maine Association of Police Executive Director Paul Gaspar before the Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety
Wednesday February 11th, 2026
LD 2090 " An Act to Establish a One-year Probationary Period for Public Safety Dispatchers"
Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety. My name is Paul Gaspar and I am a resident of South Portland.
I am speaking in my capacity as Executive Director of the Maine Association of Police, or "MAP". MAP currently represents approximately 850 municipal and county law enforcement officers and public safety dispatchers throughout the state. Today, I speak neither for, nor against LD 2090 in its current form, however I have been in contact with Rep. Bunker, its sponsor and are hopeful for amended language to be forthcoming.
It has been a great opportunity to have spoken with Representative Bunker in regard to concerns that were brought by our dispatcher members. After discussions with Representative Bunker and hearing about a proposed amendment, we would certainly be in support of this bill in its amended form.
Our concerns with the bill as originally written, is that LD2090 would create an entirely new designation and requirement for public safety Dispatchers under Title 26. However, there already exists under Title 30-A, general guidelines related to probationary periods for both municipal and county employees, as well as the specific and additional probationary period specific to law enforcement officers. Following their certification from the Maine Criminal Justice Academy.
The concern expressed by MAP on behalf of its members include potential conflict with these existing probationary periods outlined in Title 30-A would conflict with the proposed bill and create some confusion in municipalities and counties who have already instituted their own guidelines within the allowances in the existing statutes and cause confusion during their hiring processes. These would also potentially conflict with existing collective bargaining agreements that mirror the specific requirements of each of the units we represent.
After communicating with Representative Bunker, we learned that there would be an onerous process to amend existing statutes that would require considerable changes to specific sections in Titles that are specific to all public safety dispatchers in all three of the state, county and municipal segments. The amendment, if proposed, will create the probationary period under Title 26 as originally drafted, however would provide guidance that will provide for a minimum/maximum period that would be applied specifically to those defined as public safety dispatchers. This minimum maximum of no less than 6 months, no more than 12 months would continue to allow some local control and still adhere to the requirements outlined in the bill.
We believe that this would satisfy the concerns we have expressed in most, if not all matters and in that eventuality, MAP would support this specific amendment and structure of LD2090 and advocate for the committee's "Ought to Pass" vote.
Thank You for your time and I will be happy to attend the work session on this bill.
Sincerely,
Paul D. Gaspar Maine Law Enforcement Coalition/Maine Association of Police

Statement in support of
L.D. 2090, An Act to Establish a One-year Probationary Period for Public Safety Dispatchers
Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety
February 11, 2026
Senator Beebe Center, Representative Hasenfus, and honorable members of the Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee. My name is Scott Stewart. I am the Chief of the Brunswick Police Department, and the president of the Maine Chiefs of Police Association. I am providing testimony on behalf of the Association in support of LD 2090.
The Maine Chiefs of Police Association's mission is straightforward: to strengthen the working relationships among Maine's police leaders, to promote professionalism and consistent standards across the state, and to support the men and women who serve our communities every day. At the heart of that mission is a shared commitment to protecting life and property and upholding the values of our profession.
For municipal police departments, the effectiveness of our operations depends heavily on the skill and judgment of our dispatchers. They are the first point of contact for our residents, and they are the lifeline for our officers in the field. The role has changed dramatically over the years, and our training and expectations have evolved to match that reality.
Public safety communications is no longer an entrylevel clerical function. What once required a single week of NCIC training now demands approximately four weeks of classroom instruction to obtain multiple certifications. After that, new dispatchers spend four to six months in onthejob training with a field training officer, learning the policies,

procedures, and protocols needed to manage emergency and nonemergency calls for police, fire, EMS, and other municipal services. This is a complex, highstakes profession, and municipal agencies feel the impact directly when a dispatcher is not fully prepared.
Even after completing formal training, dispatchers need additional time to build confidence and proficiency. They must learn to apply complex protocols, operate advanced technology, and make rapid decisions under pressure. A oneyear probationary period ensures that dispatchers complete all required certifications, finish inhouse training, and have time to demonstrate competency beyond the structured training phase.
For a municipal police department, this additional time is essential. It allows us to ensure that the people entrusted with officer safety and public communication are fully ready for the responsibility.
Dispatchers are the first link in every emergency response. The information they gather and the decisions they make directly affect the safety of our officers and the community. Mistakes can have lifeordeath consequences.
A longer probationary period allows supervisors to evaluate performance across a full range of scenarios -- from winter storms to summer traffic, from routine calls to critical incidents. This protects the public, protects our officers, and reduces municipal liability.
Training a dispatcher is a significant investment for any municipality. When a new hire leaves early or fails to meet expectations, the department absorbs the cost in the way of overtime, staffing shortages, and the need to restart the training process.
A structured probationary period supports workforce stability. It improves retention, strengthens job satisfaction, and helps ensure that the dispatchers who remain with the department are confident, capable, and committed.
Across the public safety profession, agencies recognize that true competency develops over an extended period. LD 2090 formalizes this understanding and creates consistency statewide. It protects the public, supports dispatchers, and strengthens the operational readiness of municipal police departments.
For these reasons, the Maine Chiefs of Police Association respectfully urges the Committee to support LD 2090.

RE: LD2090-An Act to Establish a One-year Probationary Period for Public Safety Dispatchers
Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and Distinguished Legislative Members of the Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee;
My name is William Doyle. Currently I serve in the role of Executive Director for the National Correctional Employees Union (NCEU). The National Correctional Employees Union (NCEU) represents nine (9) County Correctional Units including dispatchers in the State of Maine comprising of approx. five hundred (500) members from York to Aroostook County. We have been advocating for correctional, communication, and law enforcement officer salaries and benefits since 2010 in the State of Maine.
The NCEU would like to thank the Sponsor Bunker for your efforts and support for the law enforcement community in this bill, as well as others. However, the NCEU rises in opposition to this proposed bill requiring a one year probation period.
Under the current state statue 30-M.R.S.A � 2701, employee probation periods are set at six (6) month, "Except as specifically provided otherwise by charter or ordinance...."
This proposed law change would extend the current probation period to one year, not to mention undermine collective bargaining. Probation periods, outside of law, are mandatory subjects of bargaining. Many collective bargaining agreements allow for increased probation periods and mutually agreed upon extensions. The proposed change is another example of attempting to fix a problem that doesn't exist.
If changed, the employer would be able to dismiss, suspend, or discipline employees for up to twelve (12) months without Just Cause or Cause at all. The imposed discipline or dismissal would be outside the collective bargaining agreement and not subject to the grievance and arbitration provision of the contract.
Management currently has six (6) months to decide whether an employee is a good fit or not up to the essential functions of the job. There's no good reason to extend the probation period for the hard working men and women who answer the call and are subjected to forced trauma when the phone rings. Let us not forget, Communication officers were added to the Rebuttal Presumption Disability legislation regarding Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) due to their work environment.
In closing, the NCEU would like to reiterate our OPPOSITION for LD2090 and urge the committee to vote Ought Not To Pass (ONTP). Thank you very much for your time and I'm happy to answer any questions.
In Solidarity,
